prompt: Servers ran at 70% CPU with fine latency. Traffic grew 25%, utilization hit 88%, and latency tripled.
why: Queueing delay grows like 1/(1 − utilization): near 90% small increases cause big waits.
trap: Latency isn't linear in load; plan headroom.

prompt: Finance asks why the team won't run the database at 95% CPU to save money.
why: At 95%, any burst queues dramatically. Target ~60–75% for latency-sensitive systems.
trap: Unused capacity looks like waste until you see the latency curve.

prompt: A single build runner is busy 92% of the day, and developers wait 40 minutes for builds that take 5.
tells: wait 40 minutes for builds that take 5
why: Near-full utilization means long queues. A second runner drops utilization and waits sharply.
trap: Making builds faster helps, but adding capacity off the knee helps more.

prompt: Autoscaling triggers at 90% CPU, but by the time new instances boot, latency has already spiked.
why: 90% is already past the knee; scale earlier (around 60–70%) to leave room for boot time.
trap: The autoscaler works; its threshold ignores queueing math.

prompt: A coffee shop's single barista is busy 95% of the time, and the line regularly stretches out the door even though orders take 2 minutes.
why: Near full utilization, small bursts pile into long queues; wait grows like 1/(1−ρ).
trap: Little's law links line length and wait; the knee explains why both explode.

prompt: A disk at 60% busy had 5 ms reads; at 90% busy the same reads average 40 ms.
why: Queueing delay climbs steeply past ~80% utilization.
trap: The disk didn't get slower; the queue in front of it did.

prompt: A manager plans the sprint so every engineer is booked 100%, and every urgent bug now waits days for someone to pick it up.
why: People are servers too: no slack means anything new queues.
trap: Utilization feels efficient until you measure wait time.

prompt: Consumers on one partition run at 97% capacity. A 10% traffic spike makes its lag grow without bound while other partitions are fine.
why: Above 100% arrival vs service rate, queues grow forever; at 97% there's no room for spikes.
trap: Lag looks like a Little's law question, but the instability comes from running at the edge.
